text:
Mobile phones distract students during lessons, and lessons that are interrupted by notifications take longer to get through. Students can still contact their families during breaks and at lunchtime. So schools should require students to leave their phones in lockers for the whole school day.
Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen this argument?
options: Many parents want to be able to reach their children at any time during the school day.
Schools that introduced such a rule saw exam results improve, especially among weaker students.
Phones are sometimes useful for looking things up in lessons.
Most secondary school students own a mobile phone.
Installing lockers in every school would be expensive.
solution: The argument claims phones harm learning, so evidence that removing them improved results supports it directly. The parents' wish, the usefulness of phones in lessons and the cost of lockers all count against the conclusion, and the fact that most students own phones does not affect whether the rule would help.

text:
The 24 students in a class record how many brothers and sisters they have. No two students in the class are related. The table gives the number of students in each case.

| | 0 brothers | 1 brother | 2 brothers |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 sisters | 5 | 6 | 2 |
| 1 sister | 4 | 3 | 1 |
| 2 sisters | 2 | 1 | 0 |

How many of the students' families have exactly two children?
solution: A family has exactly two children when the student has exactly one brother or sister: 1 brother and 0 sisters (6 students) or 0 brothers and 1 sister (4 students), so 10. Since no two students are related, each student is a different family. 1 brother and 1 sister makes a family of three, not two.

text:
A water tank is 80% full. Today a quarter of the water in it is used. Over the next 4 days the same amount is used each day, and at the end of the fourth day the tank is 20% full.
What percentage of the tank's capacity is used on each of those 4 days?
solution: A quarter of the water is a quarter of 80% of the tank, which is 20% of capacity, leaving 60%. Falling from 60% to 20% over 4 equal days is 40% / 4 = 10% of capacity a day. Taking a quarter of the whole tank instead of the water in it is the trap.

text:
A shop sells two fruit concentrates. Brand X is mixed 1 part concentrate to 4 parts water; Brand Y is stronger and is mixed 1 part to 9 parts water.
Which bottle gives the most drink for the money?
solution: 1 L of X makes 5 L of drink; 1 L of Y makes 10 L. Cost per litre of drink: X 1 L = 2.00/5 = €0.40; Y 1 L = 3.50/10 = €0.35; X 2 L = 3.80/10 = €0.38; Y 0.5 L = 2.00/5 = €0.40; Y 2 L = 6.20/20 = €0.31, the cheapest.

text:
Ana will drive 15 000 km in the next year in a new vehicle she is about to buy. She wants the lowest total cost for the year, including the price of the vehicle. Assume her fuel or charging cost is proportional to the distance driven.

| vehicle | cost of a full tank or charge (€) | range on a full tank or charge (km) | price of vehicle (€) |
|---|---|---|---|
| petrol | 55 | 500 | 13 000 |
| diesel | 60 | 750 | 14 000 |
| hybrid | 40 | 800 | 14 500 |
| gas (LPG) | 30 | 400 | 14 000 |
| electric | 10 | 300 | 15 000 |

Which vehicle should she buy?
solution: Running cost per km x 15 000 km, plus the price: petrol 0.11 x 15 000 = 1650, total €14 650; diesel 0.08 x 15 000 = 1200, total €15 200; hybrid 0.05 x 15 000 = 750, total €15 250; LPG 0.075 x 15 000 = 1125, total €15 125; electric 0.033 x 15 000 = 500, total €15 500. Petrol is cheapest over one year even though it is the most expensive to run.

text:
Online shopping has grown quickly, and delivery vans now make up a growing share of the traffic in city centres. Each van stops many times a day, often double-parking and holding up other vehicles. Some cities have tried allowing deliveries only outside rush hours; others have built depots on the edge of the city, where parcels are moved onto cargo bikes. Neither approach has yet been tried on a large scale, and their costs are not yet known. Yet if online shopping keeps growing, the present way of delivering to city centres will not keep working.
Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the above passage?
options: Cargo bikes are cheaper to run than delivery vans.
Cities will need new arrangements for deliveries if online shopping continues to grow.
Online shopping is the main cause of traffic in city centres.
Deliveries should be banned in city centres during rush hours.
Depots on the edge of cities have proved a failure.
solution: The passage says the current system will not keep working if online shopping grows, and describes alternatives being tried, so new arrangements will be needed. It says nothing about the cost of cargo bikes, calls vans a growing share rather than the main cause, does not recommend any particular rule, and says the depots have not yet been tried widely, not that they failed.

text: Which spacecraft carried the first people to land on the Moon, in July 1969?
solution: Apollo 11 landed Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the Moon on 20 July 1969, with Michael Collins in orbit. Vostok 1 carried Gagarin in 1961, Sputnik 1 was the first artificial satellite (1957, no crew), Gemini 4 made the first American spacewalk, and Soyuz 1 was a Soviet flight in 1967.

text: The name of the French mathematician Blaise Pascal is famously associated with
solution: Pascal's triangle sets out binomial coefficients, each the sum of the two above it; Pascal also helped found probability theory, and the SI unit of pressure is named after him. Relativity is Einstein's, logarithms Napier's, the laws of motion Newton's and the periodic table Mendeleev's.

text: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of a market economy?
options: prices set mainly by supply and demand
consumers free to choose what they buy
production targets set by a central government plan
solution: Central planning, where the state decides what and how much to produce, is the mark of a command (planned) economy, as in the former Soviet Union. A market economy coordinates production through prices, private ownership, competition and consumer choice.

text: Who directed and starred in Life Is Beautiful (1997), which won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film?
solution: Roberto Benigni wrote, directed and starred in Life Is Beautiful and also won the Oscar for Best Actor. Sorrentino directed The Great Beauty, Tornatore Cinema Paradiso, Leone the Dollars westerns, and Moretti Dear Diary.

text: Which of the following languages is NOT a Germanic language?
solution: Finnish belongs to the Uralic family, with Estonian and, more distantly, Hungarian; it is not even Indo-European. Dutch, Swedish, Norwegian and German, like English, are Germanic languages.

text: Which pair of capital city and country is NOT correct?
solution: Turkey's capital is Ankara; Istanbul is its largest city. The same trap catches many with Australia (Canberra, not Sydney), Canada (Ottawa, not Toronto) and Brazil (Brasília, not Rio). Pretoria is South Africa's administrative capital.

text: The Pritzker Prize is a prestigious international award in the field of
solution: The Pritzker Prize, awarded every year since 1979, is often called the Nobel of architecture; Italian winners include Aldo Rossi and Renzo Piano. Medicine, literature and chemistry have Nobel Prizes of their own.

text: Which of these Italian writers was never awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature?
solution: Italo Calvino, though one of the best-known Italian writers of the 20th century, never received the Nobel Prize. Deledda won in 1926, Pirandello in 1934, Quasimodo in 1959 and Dario Fo in 1997.

text: Which of these plays was NOT written by William Shakespeare?
solution: Doctor Faustus is by Christopher Marlowe, Shakespeare's contemporary, and tells of a scholar who sells his soul to the devil. Hamlet, Macbeth, The Tempest and Othello are all Shakespeare's.

text: Which island is NOT correctly paired with the country it belongs to?
solution: Corsica belongs to France (it was ceded by Genoa in 1768, the year before Napoleon was born there). Sardinia is Italian, Crete Greek, Gotland Swedish and Madeira Portuguese.

text: Who elects the President of the Italian Republic?
options: the citizens, by direct universal suffrage
Parliament in joint session, together with delegates of the regions
solution: Under Article 83 of the Constitution, the President is elected by the two chambers of Parliament sitting together, joined by three delegates from each region (one from Valle d'Aosta), for a seven-year term. Italy has no direct election for the President.

text: Which United Nations agency is responsible for international public health?
solution: The World Health Organization (WHO), based in Geneva, coordinates international health work, from vaccination campaigns to disease surveillance. UNESCO covers education, science and culture, UNICEF children, the FAO food and agriculture, and the ILO work and labour standards.

text:
Which of the following organisms have a cell wall?
1 Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium
2 Penicillium, a fungus
3 Plasmodium, the single-celled parasite that causes malaria
solution: Bacteria have a wall of peptidoglycan and fungi a wall of chitin. Plasmodium is a protist with an animal-like cell and no wall, which lets it squeeze into red blood cells. So 1 and 2 only.

text:
Which of the following happen(s) in BOTH translation and DNA replication?
1 complementary base pairing
2 formation of peptide bonds
3 formation of phosphodiester bonds
solution: Both rely on base pairing: new nucleotides pair with the template in replication, and tRNA anticodons pair with mRNA codons in translation. Peptide bonds join amino acids, so they form only in translation. Phosphodiester bonds join nucleotides, so they form only in replication. 1 only.

text: A person walks from a dim room into bright sunlight and their pupils become smaller. Which muscles contract to cause this?
options: the radial muscles of the iris
the circular muscles of the iris
the muscles that move the eyeball
solution: The iris has two sets of antagonistic muscles. In bright light the circular muscles contract (and the radial ones relax), narrowing the pupil to protect the retina. In dim light the radial muscles contract to widen it. The ciliary muscles change the shape of the lens, and ligaments are not muscles.

text:
A population of a meadow plant is divided in two when a new mountain range rises between them. Many generations later, the plants on one side flower in spring and those on the other in autumn, so they can no longer interbreed even where their seeds now meet.
Which of the following terms is/are illustrated?
1 allopatric speciation
2 reproductive isolation
3 sympatric speciation
solution: The populations split because a physical barrier separated them geographically: allopatric speciation. Different flowering times now stop gene flow even when they meet: reproductive isolation (temporal). Sympatric speciation happens without geographical separation, so it does not apply. 1 and 2 only.

text:
One base is deleted from the coding sequence of a gene, close to its start.
Which of the following could result?
1 Most amino acids after the deletion are changed.
2 The protein is cut short by a stop codon appearing early.
3 The amino acid sequence is unchanged.
solution: Losing one base shifts the reading frame, so every codon after the deletion is read differently: most following amino acids change (1), and a stop codon often appears early in the new frame (2). With the shift near the start, the sequence cannot stay the same (3 is impossible). A substitution, unlike a deletion, can be silent.

text: Which one of the following is an example of anabolism in human cells?
options: synthesis of glycogen from glucose in the liver
solution: Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller ones and uses energy. Joining glucose units into glycogen is anabolic. The others break molecules down (catabolism): starch to maltose, glucose to pyruvate, amino acids losing their amino group, fatty acids to acetyl-CoA.

text:
A baby is born with a small hole in the septum between the left and right ventricles.
Which of the following is most likely to happen when the ventricles contract?
options: Deoxygenated blood flows from the right atrium straight into the aorta.
The pulmonary vein carries deoxygenated blood.
Some oxygenated blood flows from the left ventricle into the right ventricle and back to the lungs.
The left ventricle pumps blood at a lower pressure than the right ventricle.
solution: The left ventricle contracts at a much higher pressure than the right, so blood is pushed through the hole from left to right. That oxygenated blood joins the right ventricle and is sent to the lungs again. The hole is between the ventricles, so it gives no route from the right atrium to the aorta, and the valves still work.

text:
Which of the following statements about pancreatic juice are correct?
1 It contains lipase, amylase and protease enzymes.
2 It contains hydrogencarbonate ions that neutralise acid from the stomach.
3 It is stored in the gall bladder.
4 It is released into the duodenum.
solution: Pancreatic juice carries the three main classes of digestive enzyme and hydrogencarbonate, and flows down the pancreatic duct into the duodenum. The gall bladder stores bile, which is made by the liver, not pancreatic juice. So 1, 2 and 4 only.

text:
Put these events at a synapse that uses acetylcholine in the order in which they happen.
1 Calcium ions enter the presynaptic knob.
2 Vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane.
3 An action potential arrives at the presynaptic knob.
4 Acetylcholine diffuses across the synaptic cleft.
solution: The action potential arrives first (3) and opens voltage-gated calcium channels, so calcium ions flow in (1). Calcium makes the vesicles fuse with the membrane and release acetylcholine (2), which then diffuses across the cleft to the receptors (4). Order 3, 1, 2, 4.

text:
Which of the following is/are features of a bacteriophage?
1 a protein coat around its nucleic acid
2 its own ribosomes
3 a cell membrane
solution: A bacteriophage is a virus that infects bacteria. Like all viruses it is nucleic acid inside a protein coat (capsid). It has no ribosomes, no cytoplasm and no membrane of its own; it uses the host bacterium's ribosomes to make its proteins. 1 only.

text: Which tube carries urine from a kidney to the bladder?
solution: Each kidney drains into its own ureter, which carries urine down to the bladder. The urethra carries urine from the bladder out of the body. The renal artery and vein carry blood to and from the kidney, and the vas deferens carries sperm.

text:
Which row ranks these three things found in a human muscle cell by size, biggest first?

| | biggest first |
|---|---|
| row 1 | ribosome → mitochondrion → glucose molecule |
| row 2 | amino acid → ribosome → mitochondrion |
| row 3 | mitochondrion → ribosome → amino acid |
| row 4 | mitochondrion → amino acid → ribosome |
| row 5 | ribosome → amino acid → mitochondrion |
solution: A mitochondrion is an organelle about 1-2 micrometres long. A ribosome is a particle of RNA and protein about 20-30 nanometres across. An amino acid is a single small molecule, well under a nanometre. Row 3.

text:
Which of the following statements apply to viruses?
1 They contain nucleic acid.
2 They are made of cells.
3 They can reproduce only inside a host cell.
4 They carry out respiration.
solution: A virus is nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) in a protein coat. It is not a cell, has no metabolism of its own, so it does not respire, and it can copy itself only by taking over a host cell. That is why viruses sit outside cell theory. 1 and 3 only.

text: What does \(\mathrm{3O_2}\) represent?
options: one molecule containing six oxygen atoms
solution: The subscript 2 says each molecule has two oxygen atoms; the coefficient 3 says there are three such molecules. So three \(\mathrm{O_2}\) molecules (six atoms in total, but bonded in pairs, not separate). Ozone is \(\mathrm{O_3}\).

text:
An ion \(\mathrm{X^{2-}}\) comes from an atom with atomic number \(y\) and mass number \(2y + 4\).
How many electrons and how many neutrons does the ion have?
solution: Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = \((2y + 4) - y = y + 4\); gaining electrons does not change the nucleus. The atom has \(y\) electrons, and a 2- charge means two extra: \(y + 2\).

text: Which is the balanced equation for the reaction of sodium with water?
solution: Sodium forms the hydroxide NaOH (sodium is +1, so one OH) and releases hydrogen gas. Na + H2O gives NaOH + H2 has 2 H on the left and 3 on the right; doubling the sodium and water balances it: 2Na + 2H2O gives 2NaOH + H2. \(\mathrm{Na(OH)_2}\) would need sodium to be +2.

text:
Which of these noble gases has the highest boiling point?
[Atomic numbers: He = 2; Ne = 10; Ar = 18; Kr = 36; Xe = 54]
solution: Noble gas atoms are held together in the liquid only by London (dispersion) forces. These grow with the number of electrons, because a larger electron cloud is more easily distorted. Xenon has the most electrons, so the strongest forces and the highest boiling point (about -108 °C, against -269 °C for helium).

text:
Solid sodium chloride is stirred into water at 25 °C until some of it stays undissolved at the bottom.
Which two statements are correct?
1 Water is the solvent.
2 The solution is unsaturated.
3 At standard pressure the solution boils above 100 °C.
4 Sodium chloride is a covalent molecular compound.
solution: Water dissolves the salt, so water is the solvent (1). Undissolved solid left over means no more can dissolve: the solution is saturated, not unsaturated (2 wrong). A dissolved solute raises the boiling point (3). Sodium chloride is ionic (4 wrong). So 1 and 3.

text:
For the gaseous equilibrium \(\mathrm{A + B \rightleftharpoons 2C}\), the forward reaction is endothermic and
\[K_c = \frac{[\mathrm{C}]^2}{[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]}\]
Which change increases the value of \(K_c\)?
solution: Only temperature changes the value of an equilibrium constant. For an endothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right, so (K_c) rises. Pressure and removing C move the position but not (K_c); a catalyst speeds up both directions equally and changes neither.

text: Which of the following molecules has NO overall dipole moment, even though its bonds are polar?
solution: \(\mathrm{BF_3}\) is trigonal planar with three identical B-F bonds at 120°, so the bond dipoles cancel. Ammonia (pyramidal), water and sulfur dioxide (both bent) have lone pairs that make them unsymmetrical, and in \(\mathrm{CH_3Cl}\) one bond differs from the other three.

text: In which pair of species does manganese have the same oxidation state?
solution: With O = -2 and Cl = -1: \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\) +4, \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) +7, \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}}\) +6, \(\mathrm{Mn_2O_7}\) +7, \(\mathrm{MnCl_2}\) +2, \(\mathrm{Mn_2O_3}\) +3. Only permanganate and \(\mathrm{Mn_2O_7}\) match, both +7.

text:
At 25 °C, solution X has a pH of 11 and solution Y has a pH of 9.
Which statement about their hydroxide ion concentrations is correct?
options: Y has 100 times the hydroxide ion concentration of X.
X has 2 times the hydroxide ion concentration of Y.
X has 100 times the hydroxide ion concentration of Y.
X and Y have the same hydroxide ion concentration.
X has 20 times the hydroxide ion concentration of Y.
solution: pOH = 14 - pH, so X has pOH 3 and Y pOH 5: \([\mathrm{OH^-}]\) is \(10^{-3}\) and \(10^{-5}\) mol/L. X has \(10^{2} = 100\) times more. The higher the pH, the more alkaline the solution, so it is X, not Y.

text:
25.0 mL of potassium hydroxide solution is exactly neutralised by 20.0 mL of 0.50 mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) hydrochloric acid:
\(\mathrm{KOH + HCl \rightarrow KCl + H_2O}\)
What is the concentration of the potassium hydroxide solution, in g \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\)?
[\(M_r\) of KOH = 56]
solution: Moles of HCl = 0.0200 x 0.50 = 0.010 mol, and the reaction is 1 : 1, so 0.010 mol of KOH in 0.0250 L: 0.40 mol/L. In grams: 0.40 x 56 = 22.4 g/L. 0.40 is the answer in mol/L, not g/L.

subject: Mathematics
text: Write \(\dfrac{3}{3 - \sqrt{5}}\) with a rational denominator.
solution: Multiply top and bottom by \(3 + \sqrt{5}\): the denominator becomes \(9 - 5 = 4\) and the numerator \(3(3 + \sqrt{5}) = 9 + 3\sqrt{5}\). Using \(9 + 5 = 14\) in the denominator is the usual slip.

subject: Mathematics
text: What are the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola \(y = 3x^2 - 4x + 1\)?
solution: The vertex is at \(x = -\dfrac{b}{2a} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}\). Then \(y = 3 \cdot \dfrac{4}{9} - \dfrac{8}{3} + 1 = \dfrac{4}{3} - \dfrac{8}{3} + 1 = -\dfrac{1}{3}\). The point \(\left(\dfrac{1}{3}, 0\right)\) is on the curve (a root) but is not the vertex.

subject: Mathematics
text:
In a class of 30, twelve students had a mean test score of 15 and the other eighteen had a mean score of \(x\). The mean score of the whole class was 13.8.
What is \(x\)?
solution: Work with totals, not means: the class total is 30 x 13.8 = 414 and the first group's is 12 x 15 = 180. The other eighteen scored 414 - 180 = 234, so \(x = 234/18 = 13\). Averaging the two means would ignore the different group sizes.

subject: Physics
text:
A 40 W heater is placed in a solid that is at its melting point. In 600 s, 80 g of the solid melts, and its temperature does not change.
What is the specific latent heat of fusion of the solid?
[Assume all the heater's energy goes into melting the solid.]
solution: Energy supplied = power x time = 40 x 600 = 24 000 J. Specific latent heat = energy / mass melted = 24 000 / 80 = 300 J/g. The temperature stays constant because the energy breaks bonds rather than raising the temperature.

subject: Physics
text:
An aircraft points due north and flies at 120 m/s relative to the air. A steady wind blows towards the east at 50 m/s.
What is the aircraft's speed relative to the ground, and the angle of its path east of north?
solution: The two velocities are at right angles, so add them as vectors: \(\sqrt{120^2 + 50^2} = 130\) m/s, not 170 (simple addition). Measured from north, the opposite side is the 50 m/s drift and the adjacent side the 120 m/s heading: \(\tan^{-1}(50/120)\). \(\cos^{-1}(50/130)\) is the angle from east.
